UNITED NATIONS-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION- MEMBERS OF OPPOSITION
speechtext:
1.	When opposition members of parliament are selected as delegates to the United Nations, who selects them?
2.	What duties and responsibilities have they as delegates at the United Nations?
3.	Do they serve on committees? If so, have they voice and vote?
4.	Have opposition members of parliament the right to initiate discussions and formulate policy?
5.	Are they obliged to make any kind of report to the government when they return from a United Nations meeting?
6.	What remuneration do they receive by way of (a) per diem allowance; (b) living allowance; (c) transportation Allowance?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: UNITED NATIONS-CANADIAN REPRESENTATION- MEMBERS OF OPPOSITION
speechtext:
1. The government. At the time of the San Francisco conference it was decided that the Canadian delegation should be selected on an all-party basis. Accordingly, opposition members of parliament were appointed by the government, with the approval of the party leaders concerned, to serve in the capacity of delegates to the conference. In August, 1947, prior to the second session of the general assembly of the United Nations, the practice of designating opposition members as "delegates" was discontinued on the ground that it was unfair to place members of opposition parties in a position where they would appear to be acting as spokesmen for the government. From that time opposition members appointed to Canadian delegations have been designated as "parliamentary advisers" and have thus been absolved of any appearance of responsibility for the formulation or expression of Canadian policy. In accordance with this arrangement opposition members of parliament, selected by agreement with the party leaders concerned, have served as parliamentary advisers to the Canadian delegations to the second and fifth sessions of the general assembly in 1947 and 1950 respectively.
2.	Their function is to observe the proceedings of the general assembly, to attend meetings of the Canadian delegation, and to convey to the chairman of the delegation such views as they may care to express on matters before the assembly.
3.	They do not serve on committees and thus have no voice or vote.
4.	They have the right to initiate and participate in informal discussions within the

Canadian delegation, but the responsibility for the formulation of policy rests with the government.
5.	No.
6.	(a) Nil; (b) normal actual and reasonable hotel expenses, including meals; (c) first-class transportation to and from site of conference.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, May 23, consideration in committee of Bill No. 198, to amend the Customs Act-Mr. McCann-Mr. Dion in the chair.
On section 4-Overpaid duties not returnable after six months.
Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National
Revenue):	I propose to have one of my
colleagues move an amendment which will provide for a new section 125 of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I move that section 4 of the bill be amended by deleting section 125 as set out therein and substituting therefor the following:
125. (1) Where it is established by a decision of the deputy minister, an order or finding of the tariff board or a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction that money, taken to account as duty, was paid under an erroneous construction of the law, no refund shall be made unless a written application therefor is made within six months of the date of payment, and in every other case of overpayment of duty or payment of duty in error, no refund shall be made unless an application therefor is made within two years of the date of payment.
(2)	A written request for the review of a tariff classification, an appeal to the tariff board or the institution of legal proceedings for the recovery of an overpayment of duty or a payment of duty in error shall be deemed to be a written application for the purposes of subsection one.
(3)	Nothing in subsection one or two shall affect or prejudice any refund pursuant to an application pending at the coming into force of this section.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
We are moving the amendment in connection with subsection 1, because often there are claims made against the crown for a remission of taxes going back as far as three years. We believe that that right should not be extended when there is a change by reason of a finding of the tariff board, a decision of the minister, or a judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction. We believe that permission should be fMr. Green.)
given to go back over entries for a period of six months, and if money is coming to people who have paid customs duty by reason of a change, then a remission or refund should be made there.
In other cases where there have been overpayment of duty as the result of an arithmetical error or something of that kind, the applicant shall have the privilege or right to go back for a period of two years in claiming that refund. We can readily understand that, by reason of judgments of the tariff board, there have been cases in which very considerable sums of money have been paid at a rate of duty which was higher because of the classification that the department made than the duty under the classsification made by the tariff board, and that there was money coming to certain people who had been importers. But then there arises the question who gets the benefit of the remission. The importer has likely charged up the original duty in his costs and added his profit to that. The goods have been sold to customers throughout the country, and when he gets a remission, especially if it goes back beyond a period of six months, he is getting a fortuitous gain to which we submit he is not entitled.
As an illustration I should like to mention something that happened fairly recently; it is an example of what occurs under the law as it now stands, and it will help to explain the point I have in mind. An importer took issue with a departmental ruling, and he went to considerable effort and some expense to appeal that decision to the tariff board. The departmental ruling was reversed by the board and the importer then became entitled to a refund. The company filing the claim covered three years' importations, involving a refund of slightly more than $100,000. Immediately following the announcement of the board's decision, twelve other importers, who were in no way parties to the appeal and who had not contested the department's ruling, filed claims also covering three years and varying from less than $100 to as much as $59,000. The total involved was $160,000. One importer claimed a refund of $59,290, a second $34,631.44, and two others $10,955 and $10,825 respectively. It is more than likely that these refunds remained in the hands of the claimants and were not passed on to the actual purchasers who had assumed the tax in their purchase price. Such a wide distribution would in any case be difficult for the importer to effect unless his records had been set up for such an eventuality. Furthermore there would be no obligation on him to do so, as the purchaser would have no legal right to claim any refund or any portion of

the refund made to the importer, unless of course some such clause existed in the terms of sale, which would he most unusual.
As this is a typical example, it will be seen therefore that what actually happens is that a number of importers suddenly and sometimes most unexpectedly find themselves, owing to the separate action of another, with a right to reclaim taxes paid over a period of three years and to obtain a refund, which would be in effect a fortuitous additional profit. We do not collect duties short paid by reason of an error, unless we notify the importer within a month of the time that the error was made. We feel that we should not have to go back beyond six months for remissions to importers in the case of a change in the law, or beyond two years in the event of any error on our part.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
Undoubtedly the amendment has eased the very stiff provision of section 4 of the amending bill as it stood, which I think was oppressive. In the first place, two years are now allowed in cases where payments are made by mistake. That of course was obviously necessary, because unless a man is following up his accounts month by month he might not discover the error in time. If by chance he is making his check at the end of the year he might find that the six months period had already elapsed. Subsection 2 of the amendment is also an aid, because it makes clear that a request for tariff classification and so on shall be deemed to be a written application for the purposes of subsection 1. I admit frankly that is an alleviation of the harshness of the original section; nevertheless I submit very earnestly to the minister that the reasons he has given for making this most substantial change from the three years in the original section are inadequate, and I suggest that it is creating an unnecessary hardship. The minister may say that six months is long enough. You might say that six months is long enough for an individual; nevertheless ordinary debts remain collectible within a period of six years. In our ordinary relations the usual limitation is six years. The government cut it down to three years, and now they propose in certain cases to cut it down to six months.
I suggest that the minister has given very inadequate reasons. In the first place I repudiate the idea that this section is being passed in order to prevent sharp practice, or something almost worse than sharp practice, on the part of certain businessmen. That seemed to be the argument. I think one thing we can trust our government to do is to be hard enough on individual citizens. There was a case brought up the other day
Customs Act
by the hon. member for Eglinton where it seemed to me the government department had been unnecessarily hard. Be that as it may, I still submit that to cut in two, namely to three years, the time which ordinary people are allowed in their transactions with each other is going quite far enough. I submit that the cases which the minister has given, if I understood them correctly, do not suggest any loss on the part of the government. Indeed the minister referred rather slightingly to a man exercising a right which had been in existence for more than six months. If it is a right, what is wrong about exercising a right? Nevertheless it almost seemed as if the minister were asking us to take the view that of course no reasonable man would think that anyone should exercise a right after the six months period had elapsed.
I understand that the present period was itself a reduction from a longer period. I do not know how long ago that was. But I am told that the original period used to be even longer than three years, that it was six or seven years. If I am wrong the minister will correct me. At any rate, that is as it may be; I am basing my argument on the three years. I am suggesting to the minister that nothing he has said shows that the public interest is suffering; therefore there is no need for this change, and I still hope that the minister may be prepared to withdraw the section.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when I read the amendment first proposed I thought it was pretty harsh. The amendment introduced this afternoon certainly makes it much better than what was contained in the bill as originally introduced. Still I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Greenwood to this extent, that the reduction from three years to six months in the one case is very substantial, and it seems to me that "erroneous construction of the law" would mean that it was really an error on the part of the department itself. I believe a period longer than six months should be allowed within which the importer should be permitted to make an application. I am wondering if the minister would increase that period to one year, leaving the two years in the other case. I believe that would be much more satisfactory; for it seems to me six months is pretty harsh. I imagine that in some businesses a mistake of this kind might not be discovered until, perhaps, there was some inquiry into the affairs of the company by accountants.

I hardly think the hon. member for Greenwood is being fair when he says I referred rather slightingly to some of the cases that have -come under this section; however, we will let that pass. There cannot be any injustice done to anyone, because in the great majority of cases the limitation will result in no hardship on the importer, and where any hardship does occur the governor in council may provide just relief by a refund under section 33 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.
As to the decision by the deputy minister, any such decision would be made known to importers throughout the country. The judgment of a court is published; the tariff board is equivalent to a court and -all its judgments are published. So it is not a question of taking advantage of anyone or inflicting a hardship on anyone, but I believe the revenues of the -crown should be protected to the extent that no one should make a fortuitous gain by going back two or three years. In the case I -cited, the customer got no relief, but somebody made a good deal of money.
I do not know that I can -accept the suggestion. of the hon. member for Greenwood that the period be extended to one year. This matter has been given -careful consideration by the cabinet, and the amendment that was decided upon is the amendment now proposed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
One point has occurred to me that I should like to raise; it is a matter of draftsmanship. Subsection 2 says:
A written request for the review of a tariff classification, an appeal to the tariff board or the institution of legal proceedings . . . shall be deemed- to be a written application . . .
That seems to make it perfectly clear that at the worst the importer is bound- to know what is going on, because he will have made an appeal himself. I am troubled -about

subsection 1, however, where it says-, "Where it is established by a decision of the deputy minister". Is it not possible that in- that case there might be a decision to which the importer might not -be a party in- the sense that he was notified of it? And is it not conceivable that in su-ch a -case he would not get effective actual notice of it, and that the six months might slip away before he learned of it?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Usually these matters are not confined to one person. On representations being made by -an importer that he is going to make an appeal, our office usually notifies all other importers in a similar line of business.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: That would be an appeal to whom?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: An appeal to the minister, or it may be brought before the tariff board. In -this instance if he is making an appeal for remission of customs duties it is probably on the basis that the law has been changed by -the tariff board to the extent that the goods he imported were wrongly classified and should be under another item on which the customs tariff is lower, so that having paid the higher rate he would be entitled to a refund. We say if he makes application for refund within a period of six months he comes within the law and is entitled to a remission.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I realize that, as -the minister has said, this is a decision of the cabinet, and for that reason he -proposes to stand by the amendment now before us. I would point out, however, that the reduction in time in this instance is very substantial. It is not a reduction from three years to two years or to one year; it is a reduction from three years to six months, or only one-sixth the time that was previously given. It does seem to me that if over the years three years was regarded as a satisfactory time, conclusive reasons should be given, before an amendment is adopted which might very easily deprive some company or individual of a substantial sum of money because, acting in perfectly good faith, they did not know they were entitled to it and failed to give notice. The minister has said the cabinet has decided, but after all I assume the cabinet decides on all these bills that are brought before us.
I urge the minister to reconsider his decision, or in any event to give us a positive and clear example by specific reference which would indicate the reason for such a substantial reduction. It may well be that those on -this side of the house discussing this matter cannot give specific cases in which

they think hardship would arise. In the very nature of things that information is not available to them. Before an existing legal right is taken away in this manner we should have much more information than is before us at the present time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I should like to supplement one thing that was said with respect to subsection 1. The fact is that many cases are test cases, and frequently people who are contemplating appeals will not themselves initiate those proceedings if they know someone else has taken that action, because they are waiting to see what happens. It is a proper and recognized form of procedure to await the outcome of some other case. Now, the 'likelihood is that proceedings before the tariff board or negotiations with the deputy minister-particularly the proceedings before the tariff board or an appeal to a court- will occupy all the six months before a decision is rendered. This would have the effect of precluding those who were awaiting the outcome of the test case from making any application, because the six months would have run out. The six months runs from the time of payment, not from the time of the decision being rendered. I would strongly urge, therefore, there is good ground for suggesting that the period be not reduced so substantially, that it be not reduced from three years to six months but that the minimum time should be one year.
I should like to take up another point dealing with subsection 3 of the amendment, which reads as follows:
Nothing in subsection one or two shall affect or prejudice any refund pursuant to an application pending at the coming into force of this section.
I can appreciate the purpose of this section, and I agree with it. I wonder, however, whether it is completely clear, since you have now changed the definition of the application, making it necessary for the application to be in writing. Then, in subsection 2 you say what shall be deemed to be a written application. Is it sufficiently clear what is meant by subsection 3, that is whether any form of application will be sufficient to bring it within subsection 3, or whether it must now be an application in the form referred to in subsection 2?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Subsection 3 means that any applications that have been made to date, whether written or verbal, are not ruled out.

speechtext:
What about the point with respect to the suggestion that the waiting period be six months from the date of the decision, or else a year from the date of the payment?

speechtext: Those cases would be given consideration, and in the event of undue hardship an application can still be made for a remission. Under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, that remission could be made. I may say that in practice it is not the minister or the deputy minister who makes the remissions. They make a recommendation, and the recommendation goes to the treasury board; then the remissions are made by order in council. I submit, therefore, that the interests of all taxpayers and citizens who are importers are amply protected by the present provision.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: But treasury board could not give effect to a recommendation from the minister if the statute contained the six months' limitation. Surely the treasury board could not take compassion upon someone and give him a refund if more than six months had elapsed before he made his application. I am not clear on that, but my first impression would be that even treasury board could not override a statute.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: If it were a case of undue hardship-I am not saying they could override the statute-a remission could still be made.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I want to give an example of a situation in which this section would work a hardship. In 1948 a company of mine imported a production machine from the United States. The duty on it was a substantial amount, and there was about $400 sales tax assessed against that machine. In talking about the price of the machine a year afterwards, I recalled an amendment going through this house to the effect that a production machine was free from sales tax. I took up the matter with the authorities, and we secured a refund. If the tariff board make a mistake, does it ever make a refund without an application? If this provision had been in effect at that time, we would never have secured the refund.

speechtext: The tariff board has nothing to do with refunds. It may direct one, or, by virtue of its decision, may put an importer in the position where he is entitled to a refund.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I do not wish to cross-examine the minister too closely on a question of law, because I know it is not proper to do that in the committee. As a result of an answer the minister just gave, I am a bit concerned about this matter. As I said a moment ago, I am interested in a test case, and others are perhaps awaiting the outcome of the test case before making an application in the normal way. As I see it, the amendment in its

Customs Act
present form-since most of these cases would take six months to be decided-would preclude those who were awaiting the outcome of that case from making an application for a refund. The minister has said that in case of hardship, on the recommendation of the minister or deputy minister, the treasury board may pass an order in council providing that a refund shall be made. At first sight, that would appear to take care of the type of case to which I have referred. On the other hand I should be quite surprised if, in the face of what will now be a specific provision in the act, the treasury board could in fact have such an order in council passed unless there is a general provision in the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. I should like to ask the minister whether there is a section in that act which says that, notwithstanding the provisions of any other act, in cases of hardship the treasury board may pass such an order in council.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: There is a general provision of that kind. So far as the matter of notification is concerned, all the party has to do is write a letter to the department and indicate that he proposes to appeal pending the decis-sion of the tariff board.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
The more I think about this six months' period, the more it seems to me the possibilities for great unfairness are substantial. We all admit there has to be some limit. We cannot have things outstanding for ever, but this provision would cut the time down to one-sixth. Let us consider what may happen. A man pays his rate, and he is not very well satisfied. The amount involved may not be very large, and after all there are always expenses in connection with making applications. As a matter of fact, he does not make an application. Other applications along the same line have been made, and his six months expires on a certain day. The day after the six months have expired, a ruling is made which makes it quite clear that if it had been made two days earlier he would have been entitled to a refund.
If I followed the minister, he had the feeling that that was wrong-I want to be fair in what I am saying. The minister seemed to think it was unjust to the public that other people should come in, if I interpreted him correctly.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I was just describing an incident.	.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
Very well, but I shall put my own interpretation on it, and the minister can alter it. It seems to me that to cut this down to six months is
IMr. Fulton.]
very harsh and oppressive. Six months sounds like a long time, but we all know that in business it can be a short time. Various things may happen and it may be difficult to reach a decision, particularly perhaps if the amounts involved are small, or perhaps if they are large. I suggest that the very greatest kind of hardship can arise if I have described the situation correctly. Here is a man who is in doubt. He lets the six months period elapse, and the very next day it turns out that he did have a right which is now established by the action of somebody else. I take it that the minister will say:	Why
should he profit by the action of somebody else? I think he should profit by being entitled to have his rights, according to what the law is now determined to be.
I now come back to the question of what is reasonable. I do not suggest that it should be ten years or twenty years. We all know that there must come a time when things are finished. But I suggest that three years was not an excessive time, and I suggest that one-sixth of three years is a very short and unfair time.
May I just say this also. I tried to listen carefully to what the minister said, and I did not observe any suggestion of any kind that there was any loss or hardship being suffered by the government. It did not seem to me that the minister made any case for this proposal. The more I think . about it, the more it seems to me to be harsh, oppressive and unnecessary.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just let us
compare the two procedures. If we find that there has been an error in the matter of paying customs duty, we go back not more than a month and attempt to collect where there was an error; it may be an error in computation, or it may be an error in classification. We go back a month. We allow the importer to go back six times that amount. We allow him to go back six months; and if he makes a written application within that time, his case for remission will be considered. If you are going into multiplication tables, one is six times the other; and the six months that we propose now, in comparison with the former length of time of three years, is just the same thing, namely six times.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
The minister will not wring any tears out of me by that sad story. In the first place, I am not commenting on the decision to make it a month, whether it should be that long or shorter. I am not commenting at all on that matter. All I am saying is that the minister and the department have a purse which is

limited only by the pockets of the people of Canada, whereas to the subject, to the man who is at the other end of the line, this may be a matter of vast importance. The department has thousands and thousands of cases, and they average out. The government, I presume and hope, have made a wise decision in adopting the month's limit, but that does not seem to me to have any bearing on this matter at all. It is a question of what is fair between the crown and the subject, to use those old-fashioned words. I again suggest that cutting this period down to six months is harsh, unnecessary and-I had a third word.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I know of no instance in which it has ever been passed on to the consumer. It is a gratuitous gain for the importer. He has added it on to his costs. Probably he has disposed of the goods in that length of time; when he makes an appeal he gets the money by reason of the change and in no instance that I know of has that money ever been passed on to the ultimate user of the imported article.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I have two comments to make on that, with great respect. First of all, that is none of the minister's business. He is not the keeper of the consciences of the importers; I hope their consciences are good. Nevertheless that has nothing to do with the legislation, and the fact that the minister introduces it convinces me more strongly than ever that this has been decided on an unsound basis. It is irrelevant.
The second thing is this. The minister says: I know of no cases. To me that is not very effective evidence at all. I am sorry he said it, because it implies that there are no cases. He does not know, and he cannot know. But I repeat that as a reason for cutting down this three years it is utterly irrelevant and, what is worse than that, it is improper.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I am just wondering about this amendment. I will be specific with the minister. As he knows, we are having a little bit of difficulty out in British Columbia on this interpretation of tariff item 411a as applicable to logging trucks. I think there
Customs Act
will be some proper claim that will go back a great deal longer than six months.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: The matter to which my hon. friend refers is now before the tariff board and will be heard. It was not initiated by the importers; it was initiated by the department.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Yes, of course, by the department. We were going along very well out there on the interpretation that the department originally put on it. Then, I suppose unquestionably because of abuses by some section of the industry-I can appreciate the position of the minister and the department- we suddenly find that the interpretation has been changed and they now charge duty under a different item. I am wondering if a six months period is sufficient for us if the tariff board, for instance, rules that the present decision of the Department of National Revenue is wrong. If the tariff board rules in that way, will this six months give us a chance to collect moneys that have been paid?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I think subsection 3 covers that. It says:
(3) Nothing in subsection one or two shall affect or prejudice any refund pursuant to an application pending at the coming into force of this section.
If the importers in that instance would notify the department that, pending the decision of the tariff board, they proposed to give notice or to make application for remission should there be a change, that will be sufficient to protect them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Yes; but he would have to do that on his own initiative.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I am quite certain that there are some small loggers out in British Columbia who may have bought trucks under this provision and who, if a new schedule is determined by your department, will say: Well, I guess we got hooked for it. They do not read the papers closely. I am concerned about this question whether, if they have paid the higher duties, the six months period will be sufficient.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
The minister is quite right
when he says that all importers are informed about tariff hearings. Suppose the tariff board brings out a case where another importer has1 paid too much duty and the goods in question had been imported a year before; what happens in that case?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: That is what I am complaining about.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
He would not get the refund.

Customs Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: The man who made the appeal would get it. Why should not the fellow also get it who had made importations previously?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: The six months have gone, yes. But that is not fair.

speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?

speechtext: No.

speechtext: Another thing the minister said was that if they collect less duty than they are required to collect according to the regulations, they do not go back any further than one month. I know of a case in which they went back two years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
Shall the amendment
carry?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, let me explain that. The hon, member says we go back two years. That has been in the case of fraud.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: No, it was not a case of fraud.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I want to point out to the minister that he still has not answered my two questions. He has not given me any satisfaction with regard to my question whether the public is suffering any real loss or hardship. The other thing I want to point out is that he has not answered my suggestion which I will put in this way. In a way we are here under a misapprehension. This is not an act to amend the Customs Act. It is an act for the punishment of the Canadian importer. That is practically what the minister said. He suggests that he does not know of cases in which the importer has turned back the money. Indeed, he was generous enough to say that in certain cases it might be difficult for him to do so. Nevertheless the minister gives as a reason for this proposal the strangest reason I have ever heard given in connection with the Customs Act, namely, that some people were making improper profits. He is going to condone them so long as they are made within six months, but he feels that those over six months have some special delinquency attached to them. I still maintain that this is being put forward on an unsound basis, and that the basis of six months is unfair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
There must be some difference between capital and consumer goods. I can understand that a tank car of vegetable oil

would be considered as consumer goods. But anyone who paid $20,000 or $30,000 for a logging truck would have a long memory in the matter, and would know that he paid 10 per cent, 12J per cent or 17 per cent as the case may be.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
In capital goods, where
there would be a hardship they would be taken care of by way of application for remission under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I have heard the minister's explanation, but I should like to know the actual reason for reducing the period of three years down to six months. Is it to benefit the department at the expense of the individual, or what is the real or primary purpose? What harm was done when the period was three years, when there was an erroneous construction of the law and payment was made as a consequence of that erroneous construction? What possible harm could there be in continuing the period of three years?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: My answer is that there is a loss of revenue to all the people of Canada in favour of a return of revenue to a few who have been in that position. In order to promote good business methods, I do not think it is proper that we should have to go back over a period of three years. I do not know of any private concern or insurance company that would go back that far.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
It is six
years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: No. I want to take up a word the minister has just used. The reason he gives now is somewhat different. He says now that there is a loss to the people of Canada and a gain to some Canadian citizens. But apparently there is no suggestion in his mind that this money which presumably will be recovered is money to which they have a right. Apparently we are asked to pass a measure so that the people of Canada as a whole may be able-to oppress those who otherwise would have a right. As I said a moment ago, we do not suggest it should be ten or twenty or fifty years, but we do suggest that three years is a short time. When we owe debts to each other they are not outlawed for six years, yet we are asked to outlaw this in six months. I say that three years was a more reasonable figure-you were much more reasonable in 1927 than now.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
It seems to me that the nub of the argument made by the minister in favour

of the amendment is that someone, or some people as a result of their business practice, might benefit by the fact that they would recover money which they would not pass on to someone else. There does not seem to be any other reason-because surely the government cannot complain if it is called upon to pay back what has been improperly charged.
Nothing can be payable, under the existing requirement which limits the time within which it will be paid to three years, unless there is in fact something owing as the result of a charge having been improperly made. An amendment to the Customs Act should not simply be something to relieve the government from its own mistakes, and this is what this amounts to, as it is put before us today.
While I am not suggesting that we continue this argument to the extent that the argument was continued in regard to relief of another kind to which reference was made in the house recently, I urge that we should not accept too lightly the contention that, merely because something may be done which would give to certain people a benefit they had not expected, we should deny anyone his legal rights within a sensible or reasonable time.
The minister has said that no ordinary or private business would be called upon to make a payment of this kind. The statute of limitations makes the individual liable for a period of six years. The three years now in this act is half of the period applying to a private individual; and I submit nothing has been put before the committee to show why it should be reduced to one-sixth of that time simply because of a speculative possibility that someone may gain some benefit that he would not pass on to someone else.
There is another point which comes before us at the moment, one which should not be forgotten. No doubt the minister heard what was said in the house a few days ago in another matter, upon which occasion a very clear statement was made that an amendment to an act would not have the effect of denying any legal right to anyone. It was explained to us in some detail that some legal rights had been in fact denied. The answer by the government was to the effect that it was quite possible for the opposition to have known that the effect of the bill then under consideration would be to deny such rights, in spite of the assurance that was given. I understand clearly the argument that is put forward now, but in view of the fact that reference was made in some detail only a few days ago to another case in which an amendment became operative in a way which was not fully disclosed at the time,
Customs Act
we should be assured on this occasion that there is no case within the knowledge of the government at the moment in which legal rights would be denied because of this suggested change.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: The minister's argument so far has referred to goods imported for resale. What about capital goods?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I answered that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Does it affect capital goods?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I answered that in reply to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. Where a hardship or injustice might result in connection with capital goods, an application would be accepted.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: But the measure does not say so.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Suppose at this date a case comes within the provisions of section 125 as now constituted. A person has a right within a period of three years to make application for refund. In effect, does not this amendment deny the existing right?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I should like to see anything indicating that it does not. For, unless there is something to the contrary, it applies to all cases after this date. It applies to all who are in the position of having a right to apply for refund. In order to remove all doubt in this connection, and to show that the government is not intending to penalize some who at the present time have rights, it should be clearly stated that in no way is it to be applicable to cases now in existence.
As a matter of fact I doubt whether anyone could raise a dissent. Let us suppose there is a person who today is in the position of being within the three-year period. Then the amendment comes into effect in the suggested form. Is it substantive law or is it procedural?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: If application has already been made it would come within the law as it stood.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: But if application had not been made, what happens then? They are still within the period of two and one-half years. Under the law as it is constituted today they are in position where they can make application, but this amendment will have the effect of depriving them of rights which they have had for the past two and a half years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
It would terminate their rights.

Customs Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
That being so, this would appear to be a most dangerous piece of legislation because it in effect takes away rights that individuals have at this date which are constituted rights and which entitle them to a refund. If there is to be a change in the period from three years to six months it should not cover those who today are within the three-year period under the law as it is now constituted. Otherwise it would be a confiscation of the rights of individuals affected thereby. That is going a long way. As I see it, such a section should not be passed by parliament. If there are reasons other than those already given for so abruptly changing the period from three years to six months, they should be stated.
I suggest to the minister that there be an additional subsection in section 125, or in some similar section, to the effect that these changes do not apply to any rights at present accrued, whether or not notice thereof has been given. As a matter of fact this section could easily be got around by a person giving notice, whether he believes he is entitled to pay the duty or not. By making application for a refund, that would be the end of it. The result would be a lot more work because you would have applications from everybody. At the time they paid the duty, whether they believed they were liable or not, they would simply notify you on the chance that some day they might have an opportunity of getting a refund. They would simply give you notice at the time they made the payment. Would the minister not agree to that amendment? As he says, this amendment is necessary administratively, but I suggest that it should not interfere in any way with the rights of persons as of this date under the original section 125.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Whether we are right or wrong, I think the minister will admit that we are in earnest about this matter. The minister has introduced an amendment to remedy what I think we all realize was most oppressive. Will he not let this section stand? Serious suggestions have been made and I would hope the minister would be prepared to let the section stand so that he can take another look at it. I think he realizes that the arguments we have raised are not trivial and I suggest that it might be allowed to stand.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: The minister has admitted that it is a hardship on the importer of capital goods. Would he be willing to change the amendment so that applications with respect to capital goods could still be made in the three-year period?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I do not think that I have admitted it is a hardship. In the case of hardship, consideration would be given. Capital goods could be imported and offered for resale in a short time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Why not change the amendment? Will the amendment have an effect on drawbacks?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: What is the period allowed for drawbacks?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I am informed it is two years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: It would have an effect on drawbacks.

speechtext:
Shall the amendment

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I am still waiting for an answer from the minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: We propose to allow the amendment to stand as indicated.

speechtext:

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: It seems to me that this amendment is brought in just to benefit the department. How much money does the department expect will be saved by changing the period from three years to six months? There is going to be a loss to the importer. How much loss is there going to be and how much does the department expect to make out of this drastic amendment?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: There is no way of estimating the amount.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: We are being asked to pass this bill to reduce a long-standing legal right, in fact to wipe out a long-standing legal right simply on the general statement that it will be of benefit to the department from an administrative point of view and will prevent certain fortuitous profits. We are now told by the minister that he cannot indicate the measure of saving that will come to the government as a result of this. It seems to me that this is a most improper way of doing it. Having regard to the fact that the minister has already given consideration to this matter and that the amendment does appear to be objected to, I suggest that the section should be allowed to stand, if necessary until later in the day, so that the law officers in consultation with the departmental officials may have a chance to consider the suggestions that have been made.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
No one could estimate the revenue that would be involved in a thing like this. No one can estimate the appeals that will be made to the tariff board and what

judgments will be given. It is an absolute impossibility for anybody to know the amount of money that would be involved. I may say that this amendment has been given most serious consideration over a long period of time and has been discussed with competent people in the department and in the government. We feel that to protect the revenue of the crown a period of six months is sufficient in which to give notification that an appeal for remission will be made.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Has it been discussed with any of the large importers of this country? Were they taken into the discussions?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I asked the minister whether they had been taken into consideration. Did you bring them into your discussions in order to get information from them? They certainly would not object if they did not know this was coming up.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: The minister says that they have had no objection from importers, but will he say that there have been no objections on behalf of importers? My understanding is that definite representations have been made to the minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is correct in that. What I meant was that there have been no objections by individuals. We have had some correspondence with the association.

Some years ago there was a case under the Excise Act in the province of Saskatchewan where the accused was brought before an inspector of the mounted police, who had been appointed as the investigating official under the Excise Act. The accused refused to answer certain questions that were put to him without being accorded the protection of the courts within the meaning of the Canada Evidence Act. I mention this, because in the case in Saskatchewan to which I referred, Rex v. Hicks, I was counsel for the appellant. In that case a judge of the Court of King's Bench, Mr. Justice Taylor, held that the individual had his constitutional right of refusing to incriminate himself, although not of refusing to answer provided protection was granted. My recollection is that in Nova Scotia within the last two or three years there was a judgment of the late Chief Justice Chisholm to the effect that the individual did not have his constitutional rights under a similar section, and he was not entitled to protection but had to testify. It is for that reason I ask the minister whether or not the law officers of the crown, realizing that there is a judgment of a Saskatchewan superior court to the effect that the constitutional rights are preserved under the Excise Act and there is a judgment of the appeal court of Nova Scotia to the effect that the Hicks case in Saskatchewan was wrongly decided, have concluded that the constitutional rights are preserved under the section in question.
If there is one thing we want to guard against in this country it is bringing into effect the trial of the individual by an administrative court, wherein the individual is actually under the control of the state. It is a dangerous precedent, and it is one that in the neighbouring country in recent years has brought the law into contempt. What I mean is this. The state shall not be placed
Customs Act
in the position where it may deny the individual his rights, however great the interest of the state may be for denying the citizen his constitutional freedom. It is for that reason I ask the minister this question. If we in this country want to preserve our British system, we must prevent administrative officials from securing powers to interrogate an individual, and place that individual in a position where he must become a witness against himself.

speechtext:
The accused was prosecuted before a police magistrate who dismissed the information. The crown carried it to appeal before a Court of King's Bench judge and that judge, Mr. Justice Taylor, dismissed the appeal and held that the individual had his constitutional rights to refuse to testify unless protection was granted to him. In that case I was counsel for the accused. Then I noticed that the appeal court of Nova Scotia, some two years later, gave a judgment in which it was stated by Sir Joseph Chisholm that no accused had the right to refuse to testify even though protection was not granted. As the minister will admit, the great danger with provisions such as the one in question is that the individual's rights are pared down and the hope of securing justice under our system will be denied. Administrative officials naturally like anything in the nature of change in the laws of evidence which will make more expeditious the proving of a case. This is one of those sections; it reminds me of the suggestion with regard to wire tapping, to which there has been considerable reference in the press during recent weeks. Naturally the crown officials would welcome the opportunity to tap telephone wires and telegraph wires. But I hope that, as long as the Minister of Justice is in the position he now occupies, this type of invasion of the constitutional rights of the individual will not be allowed.
I would not have withdrawn my objection to this section, as I did a few moments ago, by acquiescence, had it not been for the fact that the minister, following consultation with the law officers of the crown, gave it as his opinion that no person will be denied, under this section, the right to rely upon his constitutional right, non-incrimination. It is too bad that one of these cases was not carried to the Supreme Court of Canada
fMr. Diefenbaker.]
because, as the position of affairs now is, the Court of King's Bench has decided one way in the province of Saskatchewan and the Court of Appeal of Nova Scotia has decided the direct opposite in a similar case. I welcome the reply given by the minister that this section will not be another in this gradual invasion of the rights of the individual; because if there is one thing we need to do for the preservation of our democracy it is in this country to ensure that the rights of the individual shall not be abrogated or suspended at the caprice of the crown.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I am not clear, Mr. Chairman, just why it is necessary to repeal the original section and to re-enact this one. I do not claim to be familiar with the Inquiries Act. I certainly have not the intimate knowledge of these matters possessed by the hon. member for Lake Centre. But at first sight it would appear that the Inquiries Act confers upon the commissioner power to enforce the attendance of witnesses, to allow payment of expenses and so on. In the first place, why is it the desire to say that any person designated by the minister may conduct any inquiry and shall have the powers and authority of a commissioner appointed under part I of the Inquiries Act, which would seem to give him ample powers, and then go on, in an apparent attempt to revise the powers that he has, to provide that every person who refuses to answer any proper question put to him shall be liable to punishment on summary conviction?
That is the first question. Why is it necessary to do that? My concern about this matter arises out of this supposition. The person before whom the inquiry is being conducted seems to me to be given, by that provision in line twenty, the power to decide what is a proper question, over and above the power he would have under the Inquiries Act; simply by refusing the protection of the Canada Evidence Act and yet holding that this is a proper question, he exposes the witness to prosecution and punishment on summary conviction. I doubt if the witness would have any recourse. If the commissioner said: "This is a proper question and it is not one where you are entitled to the protection of the Canada Evidence Act," then the witness must answer or his refusal to answer, it seems to me, is automatically bound to be followed by fine under the summary convictions act. So I wonder why it was necessary to put that provision in, when the Inquiries Act would seem to give the necessary powers already?

Mr. Chairman, I must confess there is a good deal of point in what the hon. member says. However, I think no great problem is posed here, because it is much simpler to say in the present bill that the persons conducting an inquiry under it shall have the powers of a commissioner under the Inquiries Act. This avoids repeating quite a long list of sections in the present bill. But when it gets down to specifying for those who might be disposed to disregard these provisions what the penalty should be, then I think there is nothing contrary to good practice when we indicate in the Customs Act just what those penalties are. They cannot be stated in clearer or fairer terms. He who runs may read:
Every person who (a) fails, without valid excuse, to attend an inquiry or investigation as required under this section,
(b)	fails to produce any document, book or paper in his possession or under his control, as required under this section, or
(c)	at any inquiry or investigation under this section
(i)	refuses to be sworn or to affirm, or to declare, as the case may be, or
(ii)	refuses to answer any proper question put to him by the person conducting the inquiry or investigation,
is guilty of an offence and is liable, on summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding four hundred dollars and not less than twenty dollars.

Customs Act
That is, a gentleman who is conducting an inquiry cannot proceed to penalize summarily. The person affected must be taken before a proper judicial official who has jurisdiction on summary conviction. Then the person affected can see, by reference to the legislation, he is exposed to a penalty not exceeding the amount specified.
Admitting the force of the argument by the leader of the opposition, I do not see how very great exception can be taken to the provision because it is spelled out here in a manner which I suggest is desirable. These penalties Should be in the Customs Act, rather than in some other act to which a person reading the Customs Act would have to refer.

speechtext: In view of the rather far-reaching nature of this section I wonder if the minister could explain in some detail the reasons for this amendment? I would prefer to hear his explanation before I make some comments I wish to make on this section.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
This amendment makes it possible to provide sufferance warehouses for the convenience of highway or air transport. The lack of such warehouses has been an obstacle to highway and air transport, as well as creating administrative inconvenience at Canadian customs ports. The amendment

spells out the obligations which up to the present have been stipulated only in the bonds taken from the operators of sufferance warehouses where such persons were authorized to operate such warehouses under regulations and provisions of the act.
The actual practice is to have goods arrive by truck at the frontier point where they are cleared and then trucked to the interior destination. This amendment would permit clearance either at the frontier point or at the interior point and thus relieve the present congestion at the frontier. The present system is to have goods come to border points like Windsor, Fort Erie, Niagara Falls or hundreds of other points, where they have to be unloaded, an appraisal made, the customs duty paid, either by the person in charge of the transport or more likely by a customs broker, and then reloaded on Canadian-owned trucks for delivery to the point of destination.
Under this amendment the motor or air transport companies would themselves institute sufferance warehouses at interior points where the customs officials would supply the facilities for the appraisal of the goods and the collection of the customs. Let it be understood that the warehouses would not be built by the government. They would be licensed and bonded by the government. I submit that this is simply an evolution of transportation which has been taking place over the past few years.
It is true objections have been raised, on behalf of the railroads in particular, that this would mean a loss of business to other carriers. I submit that there would not be any loss. The practice is not to transfer from the truck coming to the border to a railroad for shipment to the point of destination, but to transfer to another truck. Take goods coming to a point like Hamilton, say from Philadelphia. These goods would cross the border at Fort Erie or Niagara Falls and under the present practice would have to be unloaded, appraised, reloaded and then they would go on after the customs duty had been paid. If this amendment goes into effect the officers at the point of entry would place a seal on the truckload of goods which would then go to the warehouse at Hamilton operated by a trucking company or a combination of trucking companies. Our appraisal officers would appraise the goods at the warehouse and collect the duty. As I said, there have been some objections, such as those from the Ship-by-Rail Association of Canada, but I think they can be well answered.
I hope hon. members will not confuse these two phases of trucking in bond as there is S0709-221
Customs Act
only one referred to in this amendment. The other phase was the trucking in bond that took place during the war where a truck would enter Canada, say at Niagara Falls or Fort Erie, cross the southern part of Ontario and leave Canada at Windsor and on to Detroit or whatever point in the United States it was destined for. That was an international arrangement between Canada and the United States that terminated at the end of the war. This second arrangement has to do with the setting up of sufferance warehouses under which the customs department will supply the needed facilities to -carry on the business.
I shall attempt to answer any further questions that are asked, but I think what I have said will serve as an introduction.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
It is clear from the explanation given by the minister that the primary intention of the amendment is to provide for the delivery by trucks of goods to sufferance warehouses. It is true that -the amendment includes air transport as well, but there are obvious reasons why it could not apply in the same way to air transport. A -truck could come right through to a sufferance warehouse whereas an aircraft must land at an airport. It is very unlikely that sufferance warehouses of -a size to deal adequately with the kind of distribution contemplated would be constructed at many airports, certainly at this time.
For that reason I think it would be well to direct our minds particularly to the effect of this amendment upon transport by highway. As the minister has pointed out, there is a very -clear distinction between the subject matter of the amendment now before us and the practice -carried on during the war whereby bonded trucks were allowed to pass through Canada from a port of entry to a port of exit. This practice led to certain discussion at that time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
The fact is, the course indicated by the minister in his remarks with regard to reloading on Canadian trucks would be the more likely one to follow, because very much larger trucks are being used in the regular transportation of goods of this kind in the United States than in Canada. Some of these trucks run to 50 or 55 tons, and even more. At the present time such trucks could not and should not use some of our highways. In fact many of these trucks would create a very real danger to the bridges on a number of our highways. For that reason the present provision is one that has results which are rather parallel to the results that followed from the action taken in regard to the bonding of goods on trucks in transit from one border point to another, which came up for discussion during the war and immediately afterwards.
At that time objection was taken, as the minister will recall, to the passage of trucks in that way not only by the railway companies but also by certain provincial jurisdictions. The minister will recall that it was pointed out at that time that these very large trucks were damaging our roads to an extent that made it a very real problem to maintain roads for ordinary truck and motor operation. To some extent the same danger would be repeated by any provision which encouraged the entry into Canada of these very large trucks. I would certainly agree with the minister and anyone else who suggests that we should adjust ourselves to changing events and the improvement of transportation methods. The first requirement, however, in dealing with changes in transportation methods is to make sure that our facilities for handling those transportation methods are adequate to the task. I believe that right across Canada we are rapidly improving our general situation with respect to highways.
The fact remains, however, that no matter what general improvement has taken place we have not yet the same network of carefully levelled highways suitable for the very large trucks that are being used in the United States today. Therefore I suggest that is a

reason, apart from some of the other reasons I shall mention, why it would not be wise to make this amendment at this time. The amendment would encourage the movement of such trucks into internal ports in Canada, in many oases over highways which would be seriously damaged by the weight of such trucks moving often in great trains.
Then I come to another aspect of the problem. There is a great difference between bonding a freight car and bonding a truck. A freight or baggage car travels over clearly defined routes. The car having been bonded moves on a railway right of way which is under fairly constant supervision, and which is subject to a measure of observation and checking that would not apply to a truck once it had passed the border. May I say at once that I am not in any way reflecting on the good faith of any of those well established trucking organizations which may believe that this would be a convenience. Nevertheless it must be remembered that our customs officials, expert and courteous though they are, have no crystal glass in which they can gaze to determine whether the people operating a particular truck are going to conform exactly with the regulations or follow a particular course.
It is possible for trucks to depart from a' direct route in a way that is not possible when goods are being moved by railway transportation. Moreover it is possible for trucks to be opened in a way that would be most unlikely in the case of railway transportation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: There is the same type of seal on them as on railway cars.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
The Minister of National
Revenue is too practical and has too good an understanding of the construction of trucks to be unaware of the possibilities of seals not being effective on trucks where they would be very effective on railway cars. Very little imagination suggests that there are many ways in which it would be possible to avoid the effect of sealing unless one were going to seal a truck with such a bond of wires that it would almost look like a bird cage. In saying that, I repeat that I am not impugning the good faith of any of those who may be applying for concessions of this kind. I suggest, however, that it must be obvious to every hon. member that a truck passing a border point, and having received a seal, would be able to do many things that would not be possible in the case of a railway freight car.
I think it must be obvious to everyone that a very extensive problem of policing and supervision is involved, which would mean the requirement of a very much larger number of men than are now employed for tasks

of this kind, in order to be reasonably sure that there was no infringement of regulations of this nature.
Then there is another problem, of course, not related to the question of the good faith of any of the truckers who may be carrying out this task. There is an invitation to interference with the operation of trucks, which does not exist in the case of a railway car or any other method of transportation. I think there are a number of reasons why the members of this house should be very cautious about passing an amendment which would invite a type of bonded transport which will create increased difficulties for the customs service, which will increase the possibility of evasion, and which will provide some encouragement to the present descendants of the highwaymen of old. These are very real considerations which should not be lightly brushed aside.
I suggest also it should be remembered that this change is not going to affect a great many communities. It will affect those large communities close to the border, where there will be a possibility of breaking load and perhaps effecting delivery a little more rapidly than can be done by rail. In view of the fact that the number of places that could benefit would be comparatively limited I think great caution should be exercised in adapting an amendment of this kind, when in this particular case there might also be great uncertainty as to whether it could become effective in any event. I would remind the minister that whether or not there was agreement on the course followed, at least one province did take action in regard to the movement of bonded goods by truck transport. That decision was taken because of the damage being inflicted upon the highways of that province without any compensating advantages which would indicate that it was not wiser to have those same loads carried by rail. This amendment may invite similar action. It might also raise very real questions as to whether it is desirable to encourage the entry into Canada of these very large trucks at a time when there is a real shortage of the steel and cement needed for the improvement of our highways. Right across Canada today the construction of cement-surfaced highways is being held up because of the shortage of steel and cement. Steel, nails and cement are required not only for the construction of new highways but also for the repair and maintenance of existing highways. No matter what arguments may be put forward as to the desirability of an amendment of this kind at some future date, in addition to the other reasons I have given the need to conserve our highways as much as possible in view of 80709-2214
Customs Act
the shortage of these supplies is such that I suggest this is not the appropriate time to bring in an amendment which will invite heavier traffic of this nature on our highways.

speechtext:
I do not wish to reply to the leader of the opposition, but I wonder if he contends that this amendment would supersede the traffic laws of the province of Ontario or any other province. I do not believe it would supersede any traffic laws or regulations of any province. This is for the benefit of those provinces which agree that United States trucks may come there, and which provide the sufferance warehouses where the goods may be delivered. As the leader of the opposition rightly said, this does not provide for trucking in transit. In that connection the laws of the United States go much further than ours. According to their laws Canadian trucks may go through the United States in transit in bond. That is the case with trucks from all provinces, even though some Canadian provinces have not granted reciprocal rights. An example of this traffic is the transportation by Canadian trucking companies of automobiles manufactured in Ontario to markets in western Canada. They go through United States territory, and have permission to do so. We are not going as far as that here, in spite of the fact that article 5 of the general agreement on trade and tariffs, which we have signed, provides that there shall be freedom of transit through the territory of each contracting party via the routes most convenient for international transit. Because of that obligation we are now discussing the matter with the province of Ontario, but there is nothing in this bill covering trucking in transit. It only has to do with warehouses. I believe that if we do not go some distance in granting reciprocal rights to the United States trucking industry there is some danger that we may lose the right we

Customs Act
now enjoy to have our trucks go in transit in bond through the United States, a right we need in connection with western Canada. I do not think we are going very far here; and moreover this legislation cannot supersede or take the place or reverse the effect of the traffic regulations or laws of any province.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: First of all, there is no suggestion that this supersedes any existing provincial law. The only case where the provinces so far have been called upon to *deal with this problem is in connection with the movement of goods in bond in transit through Canada from a port of entry to a port of exit.
