speechtext:
We had it on the Alaska
highway, too, during the war.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
And it applied also to the
Alaska highway. As has been pointed out, and as I pointed out in my opening remarks, this is not on all fours with that except to the extent that this does deal with the possibility of the entry into this country of the same type of trucks which were causing a very serious problem in the other case. It is all very well to say that we have signed some international agreement which calls for extending transport facilities through the adjoining territories of the countries signing this agreement. Common sense, however, will obviously impose the requirement that all international agreements of that kind shall be subject to appropriate restraints, having relation to the surface of the highways and the strength of the bridges over which the trucks must pass.
At this time, so far as I am aware, there is no provincial law of any province which would deal with the situation. Certain provinces were called upon to consider the effects of another provision which related to transporting goods in bond from one port to another at the boundary. I repeat my point, and the minister himself has indicated that one of the main effects of an amendment of this kind would be to avoid the necessity of breaking a load at the border and reloading it in smaller trucks. I am suggesting that is a very desirable result. I am suggesting also that it will be a very desirable result if these are Canadian trucks. Still further am I suggesting that at this time, when there is a shortage of cement and all other repair materials, we would be well advised to see that our rails are used as much as possible during this period of national emergency. For these reasons I intend to oppose section 11, and the effect of the amendment.
tMr. Lesage.]

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I wish to say a few words on this subject. First of all, I wish to congratulate the government on putting this section in the bill. I think it is something that has been needed for quite a while. I want to speak generally about the matter just now, and then I shall go into greater detail at another time. I was not at all impressed by the remarks made a moment ago by the leader of the opposition, when he spoke about the trucking industry destroying our roads.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I did not speak about the trucking industry destroying the roads. I spoke about the fact that in the United States today we see great trucks running up to fifty and fifty-five tons being used. It was those trucks to which I referred, which damaged our roads in the past and would damage them today until we have an opportunity of creating road surfaces and bridges adequate to handle them.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I am not going to bicker
over terms used. The inference left was that heavily loaded trucks would destroy the roads. In the sense that they were overloaded, I would agree. We had an experience with that in the province of Alberta, particularly during the war and the building of the Alaska highway. Some very large trucks came up from the United States carrying exceedingly heavy loads, big steel girders and steel pipes that were going into the northern territories. They did not destroy our roads to the extent one would gather from a reading of the leader of the opposition's words. Every province, Mr. Chairman, as has been pointed out, has laws regulating the weight of the traffic passing over its highways.
This difficulty has been overcome in a number of ways. We have been steadily improving the construction of our highways. Improvement has been made in the construction of the trucks. It is now possible to carry a twenty or thirty-ton load over a road and not do so much harm as it used to do. Some provinces are requiring that the load be spread over a greater number of axles so that the weight will be more uniformly spread over a greater road surface. This helps to maintain our roads. I am in favour of maintaining our roads, but I am not in favour of delaying this type of legislation any longer. I believe it has been delayed long enough.
I was quite impressed by the minister's remarks when he said he thought we should adjust ourselves to the changing times, particularly as that applied to transportation. It seems to me that this country has been very backward in adopting the more modern

forms of transportation. Perhaps we have not got enough of-I was going to use the term used in the United States-express highways. When one travels over those roads, particularly between Detroit and Chicago, one can see the tremendous advantages transportation has in the U.S. over Canada. There is a tremendous amount of traffic hauled over those roads. It is true, of course, that in that particular instance the road is built to carry those loads. But we must adapt ourselves to these changing times. In Canada we are not doing that very rapidly. It is true that we have started on the proposal to build the trans-Canada highway, but that is going to take at least seven years-I venture to say even longer. Surely, we are not going to wait for that length of time to adjust ourselves to these new types of transportation.
I was not very impressed with the remarks made by the leader of the opposition concerning the difficulties of bonding a truck. A moment ago it was pointed out by the member for Montmagny-L'Islet that our trucks now go through the United States in bond. For the many years I have enjoyed being a member at Ottawa, Mr. Chairman, with the exception of 1942-1946, I have driven every year through the United States on my way home. I have seen the advantages of Canadian trucks going through the United States in bond. Why we should not give the United States that same privilege, I do not know. It would have been very embarrassing for us if the United States had not extended that privilege, because we have no transcontinental road running east and west in Canada. We would have been up against a very difficult proposition if we had not enjoyed that privilege. I believe we should reciprocate, and give the United States the same advantage if they desire it.
The bonding of trucks is not difficult. Those trucks all go through a port of entry, and they can be sealed there just as efficiently as a box car. No one is going to say that a box car has never been broken into. It may happen in the odd case with a truck. Most of the business firms who are employing large trucks in their service are reputable companies. The suggestion that they are highway robbers is outrageous.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, nothing more
remote from what I said could be imagined than the statement just made by the hon. member.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I never said that the hon. member said that. I am just saying that to suggest that any of these reputable trucking firms could be accused of highway robbery, such as we used to have in the old days-
Customs Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it should be possible for an hon. member to conduct the argument without getting so far from the truth as has the hon. member at the moment and without creating an inference that has no relation to what I have put forward in my contention.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I am sorry if the hon. member thinks that I was referring to him.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Oh, well-

speechtext:
Of course, if he inferred that they may be highway robbers, then he can take that as he likes.
I want to ask a question or two with regard to the sufferance warehouses. It is understood that these warehouses will be constructed where there are now custom-houses?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Yes. They will be constructed at frontier points and in cities where there are already custom-houses.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Border points?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I said frontier points or border points, and in cities where there are already custom-houses. But they will not be constructed by the government. They will be constructed by the transport people. All this bill does is to say that in the event of the transport people's building warehouses, we will be prepared to make regulations and service the warehouses. Let me read the provision:
The governor in council may make regulations for the appointment of sufferance warehouses in which goods arriving by railway, highway or air transport may be stored before entry, when such goods have been duly reported.
Then section 2 makes an amendment which says that the keeper of the warehouse is to be liable for the duty. We hold him liable. If he puts the goods in the warehouse there, we hold him liable. Then we have set out the application and a provision with reference to the storing of goods. All of this talk with reference to the highways, although it is relevant in a manner to the whole question, is not relevant to this particular amendment. That is a matter for the provinces to deal with. If the province of Ontario says, "You cannot put a fifty-ton truck on our highway; the maximum is twenty tons or twenty-five tons", then all well and good. The trucking people will have to take that problem up with the various provinces. The provinces will, I presume, have a right to put on any licence fee that they want to. But we believe that this is a part of the evolution of transportation that should be taken care of, and we believe that we should take time by the forelock and tell these people:	If you are
going to build these warehouses, pay for them and operate them, we will provide the

Customs Act
facilities for the examination of your goods there, under certain conditions. You are to be responsible for them. You are to see that the duty is ipaid. You are to apply for a licence and you will get that licence; and it is just a matter of giving them the facilities at these points where the warehouses are built. The other problems are entirely ones as to which they, the transport people, will have to deal with the several provinces.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I think the trucking industry will appreciate that. What I had in mind when I asked that question was that the trucking industry would be allowed to build their warehouses wherever they saw fit, provided there was enough traffic to warrant it, and then the government would provide a customs official at that point; but that the trucking industry themselves-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: But there will be what are commonly known as common warehouses. We would not provide facilities for every trucker that is going to have a warehouse; but when a combination of them go together, we would.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I understand that. For
instance, there would be one in Calgary and one in Edmonton; and there would probably be one in Lethbridge. I am speaking of my own province because I know that one better than any other. There would probably be one in Camrose where there is a custom house already. I think that would cover any objection that the transport concerns may have in regard to this. In fact, I think I can assure the minister that they are quite pleased that he is taking the progressive step that he is taking in seeing to it that these sufferance [DOT]warehouses are being built.
Once again may I say that I do not think there is any danger of over-abuse of the privilege because there is sufficient inspection now in progress to look after any safeguarding that is necessary.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: On a matter of privilege, in the event that my words may have been in any way open to the surprising interpretation placed upon them by the hon. member who has just spoken, I wish to make it clear-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I cannot hear what the hon. member is saying.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I say that in the event that it is at all possible that my words may in any way have been open to the surprising interpretation put on them by the hon. member who has just spoken, I wish to make it quite dear that when I was referring to the possibility of practices developing in regard to interference with the trucks, I was not

suggesting interference by the trucking companies but rather interference with the trucks themselves by others.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I cannot help viewing with
alarm section 11 of Bill No. 198, because I feel a certain amount of international business will be taken away from the railways. Certainly this is not the time to take business from our Canadian railways.
I agree with the minister when he says that one cannot set back the wheels of progress, and we realize that we are in a period of transition, so far as transportation is concerned. But at this particular time I wonder if it is wise to make these concessions to the American truckers. I wonder if we are not depriving Canadian railways of business which is legitimately theirs.
I notice further in the minister's remarks that he said that goods coming in by truck are, after examination at the border, loaded into Canadian trucks.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
They are continued on in
the American trucks.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: It continues on in the American trucks?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: Then one of my worries has been dissipated by the minister's remarks.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps the
hon. member would permit me to interject the statement that a great number of Canadian truckers truck goods into the United States. They have the right to do so. Then they come back, loaded with American goods for Canadian importers.
I have before me a list of trucking companies actively engaged in the transportation of package freight as between the United States and Canada. They are: Consolidated Truck Lines, Toronto; Colville Cartage Company, Toronto; Direct-Winters Transport, Toronto; International Cartage Company, Windsor; Maislin Bros. Transport, Montreal; Bingaman Motor Express Company Incorporated, Montreal; Montreal and New York Express Limited, Montreal; Lavigne's Red Wing Express, Montreal; Dench of Canada Limited, Calgary; Canadian Freightways Limited, Calgary; Smith Transport, Montreal; Seattle-Vancouver, B.C. Motor Co. Limited, Vancouver and British Columbia-Seattle Transport, Vancouver.

I do not believe that is a full list of the big trucking companies carrying package freight from Canada to the United States, and coming back with return loads. Those people, of course, would continue with their Canadian trucks to the point of destination. And in the event that it works the other way, American trucks which come into Canada would go to their point of destination, probably pick up a load in Canada and take it back to the United States.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
While I am pleased to have
that information, I think it proves my point that these international trucking concerns are interfering with the express and freight carried by the railways. Has a survey been made, or has there been any estimate as to the loss of revenue to Canadian railways as a result of allowing these trucks to come through the border in bond, to points in Canada?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I do not know that a survey has been made with reference to that. However I can say, on the assertion of prominent trucking companies, that as a result of what happened last summer during the railway strike, at which time the truckers carried on the business of moving package freight and other freight in this country, they did retain about 35 per cent of that new business. I point that out to show that they are not an unimportant factor in the transportation business of our country.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
Have the C.P.R. and the
C.N.R. made representations opposing this change?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: No, they have not.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
I heartily congratulate the hon. member for Bow River upon the remarks he made this afternoon concerning section 11 of Bill 198. The movement of goods by bonded truckers along the Alaska highway means much to us in the north, where transportation facilities are limited, indeed. I believe every consideration should be given to the transportation of goods by truck in remote areas, and I congratulate the Minister of National Revenue upon having introduced this amendment to the Customs Act.
I do not agree with the remarks of the leader of the opposition respecting difficulties in sealing trucks carrying bonded goods, especially along the Alaska highway. I have noted for some time the manner in which these trucks have been sealed, and' I know that the trucks operating along the Alaska highway can be sealed as securely as any railway box car. These trucks are sealed with Canadian customs Tyden seals which are numbered, and each one of which must be accounted for. Therefore I cannot see
Customs Act
any reason why any freight in bond should be pilfered or stolen. I hope every encouragement will be given to these truckers in the north country, and especially in the remote areas of the Yukon Territory, northern British Columbia and other parts of Canada. It means a great deal to those of us who live up there to have this service.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: The minister referred to the different trucking companies employed in this kind of business, and referred particularly to Dench of Canada Limited. Is not Dench, in Calgary, owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway? If that is true, then the C.P.R. is trucking goods into the United States in the manner which has been described.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I must admit I do not know anything about the ownership of Dench of Canada Limited.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I have one or two questions. The minister said, as I understood him, that there had been no representations from the railways.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: I corrected that. I said there had been representations from the Ship-byRail Association.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext: What discussion was there with the interested parties? The minister referred to the trucking association. Was there any discussion with any other interested parties?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CLARIFY ACT AND TO FACILITATE ADMINISTRATION AND ENFORCEMENT
speechtext:
Personally, I have had discussions only with the secretary of the Ship-by-Rail Association. There have been other representations. Here is a communication from the Canadian Retail Federation which says:
Dear Dr. McCann:
I have been instructed to tell you that the Canadian Retail Federation view with much satisfaction the contents of the House of Commons Bill 198, section 11, by which provision is made for goods to be brought into the country under bond and by highway transport.
The federation is of the opinion that this will be helpful to the retail trade, and we wish to express our appreciation for the action that has been taken to make this possible.
Yours truly,
E. F. K. Nelson General Manager, Canadian Retail Federation
Then there is one from the recording secretary of the Brotherhood of Railway Carmen of Ontario, expressing opposition to Bill No. 198. Then there is one from the hon. member for Nipissing. There is also one from the Ship-by-Rail Association, to which I have

Customs Act
referred already. Then there is one from the Canadian Industrial Traffic League under date of May 14, reading:
The Canadian Industrial Traffic League, national organization of industrial traffic managers, has noted with satisfaction the intention of the government, as set out in Bill 198 currently before the house, to recognize by legislative action the principle of permitting the entry into Canada in-bond of shipments by highway transport.
The league has been on record in the past as favouring this principle which will make it possible for importers to clear highway transported goods at Canadian interior points.
On behalf of this organization which represents many of the companies interested in this principle, I take pleasure in bringing the above views to your attention.
Yours very truly,
The Canadian Industrial Traffic League,
H. A. Mann,
.	General Secretary
There is another one from the Canadian Importers and Trading Association, under date of May 14, addressed to myself and reading:
Dear Dr. McCann:
Members of this association were delighted to see that you propose to amend the Customs Act so as to allow goods to enter the country in highway trucks in bond.
We feel that this change in the act, when translated into practice, will be of very great benefit to the import trade of Canada and wish to express this association's hearty approval of the proposed change.
Yours sincerely,
Canadian Importers and Traders Association, Inc.
H. C. MacKendrick,
General Manager
I do not think it is necessary to place all this correspondence on the record. I am just taking the letters as they are on the file. They all appear to be letters in appreciation of the action that has been taken. They are from influential bodies. Here is one from the Canadian Automotive Transportation Association, Toronto, under date May 11, and reading:
I wish to express the sincere appreciation of the Canadian trucking industry for the action which you have taken, on behalf of the government, in introducing Bill 198 amending the Customs Act to permit "in bond" trucking.
With regard to the Customs Act, it has long been the view of this association that, in the language of the bill it was "necessary to extend the power to cover goods specifically arriving by highway."
The amendment to the act places all forms of transportation on an equal footing with regard to "in bond" transportation and establishes for the shipping public the same privileges in the movement of international traffic by the several media.
If it develops that this bill is to come before a house committee at which witnesses will appear, it is the desire of this association to have a representative present to register the trucking industry's strong support of the bill.

The other letters on the file are my replies to the different people who have written.

from what the minister has said that this privilege will be granted to all trucking companies. The minister read quite a long list and I take it it will be general.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: DEFINITION OF CANADIAN STANDARD YARD AND POUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the primary standards of weights and measures are now defined in the Weights and Measures Act. The unit of length is fixed with reference to a specific bar, and that of the Canadian pound by reference to a specific weight of metal. In defining the primary standards to be used, it is obviously desirable that there be uniformity of standards all over the world. On the other hand, it must be realized that any given bar of metal or a given weight will vary slightly from time to time. It is quite true that the change is very slight in any one year. It is so slight it is almost impossible to measure it. But over a period of decades the amount of change may be of practical significance.
The present Canadian fundamental standards of length and mass were received from the British government in 1873, when our first Weights and Measures Act was passed. They were accurate copies of the imperial standards which, at that time, were representative of the finest technique in precise measurement. In the intervening eighty years there has been a great deal of advance in the science of metrology, including the establishment of special laboratories in all the principal countries of the world for making precise measurements, such as our own division in our national research council laboratory.
This development has led to the recognition of the fact that the old standards of yard and pound are changing very slightly. On the other hand, the international metre and kilogram standards established at the international bureau of weights and measures at Paris have been found to be remarkably constant. For these reasons it was suggested, at the royal society empire scientific conference in 1946, that the standard yard be referred to the international metre and the pound to the international kilogram by fixed ratios. If all nations agree to the same ratios between yard and metre, and between pound and kilogram, then there will be only one standard length and one standard weight. Therefore, even if there should be very


slight changes in these fundamental standards in the course of centuries, no difficulty will arise in international commerce and international science.
Actually in the United Kingdom there is an order in council of 1898 that defines the ratio of the pound and the kilogram, and there is a similar act in the United States giving the same ratio. This bill proposes to establish this same ratio for Canada. This ratio is the same as the present Canadian standard pound, so that there would be no change except that any future change of the actual standard pound would be of no consequence. The ratio used in the bill for the yard and the metre is between that actually applying to the standard yard of the United Kingdom and the United States, and is that recommended by the royal society empire scientific conference. It has the endorsation of many standardizing bodies and scientific societies, both in the countries of the commonwealth and in the United States.
By this bill units of measurement will be based on standards, the stability of which has been proved as nearly perfect as can be attained. The second part of the bill establishes that the operation of maintaining the standard yard and the standard pound at the proposed values is the responsibility of the national research council, and that they will supply reference standards calibrated in terms of the fundamental standards to other government departments. That is a logical step to take. It will be recalled that in the national research council legislation one of the powers of the council has to do specifically with maintaining units of weight and measurement.

speakeroldname: Hon. Siuari S. Garson (Minister of Justice) moved

subtopic: STATUTORY REMISSION OF SENTENCES, NORTHWEST AND YUKON TERRITORIES, AND CUSTODIAL CARE, ALBERTA
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement at this time?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: STATUTORY REMISSION OF SENTENCES, NORTHWEST AND YUKON TERRITORIES, AND CUSTODIAL CARE, ALBERTA
speechtext:
I will make a short statement, Mr. Speaker. The parliament of Canada, under its authority over the subject of *criminal law, has passed in the Criminal Code a statute which defines the various crimes and offences in this country and prescribes the penalties which must be imposed upon those who have been convicted of such crimes and offences. It also provides for the manner in which such sentences shall be served.
For the purpose of considering the present bill, the governing provision here is section
3476	HOUSE OF
Prisons and Reformatories Act 1056 of the Criminal Code which provides that everyone who is sentenced to a term of imprisonment of less than two years shall, if no other place is expressly mentioned, be sentenced to imprisonment in the common jail of the district, county or place in which the sentence is pronounced, or if there is no jail there, then in the common jail which is nearest to that locality. It is in line with that provision in the Criminal Code that the Prisons and Reformatories Act is passed. It actually is an extension of this idea which is set out in section 1056 of the Criminal Code. The Prisons and Reformatories Act provides, in part I of it, for provincial prisons and reformatories generally. Then in parts II to IX the act is made applicable to different types of reform institutions in the various provinces, part II dealing with Ontario, part III with Quebec, part IV with Nova Scotia and so on.
Clause 1 of the bill before the house has to do with a provision in part I of the Prisons and Reformatories Act-that is the part which has a general application to all the provinces-for a statutory partial remission of sentence for good conduct. To grant such a remission as this is the normal procedure in most jails in the provinces of Canada. It is considered-and that is the reason why we put this clause 1 into this biff-that the same privilege should be applied to prisoners in the Northwest and Yukon Territories. The granting of this remission for good conduct is provided for in sections 18 to 21 of the Prisons and Reformatories Act. These sections do not have effect until they are proclaimed, and up until the present time they have not been proclaimed in the Yukon or Northwest Territories.
The present section 18 provides that if there is in any province a prison of such a character as to render practicable the administration of remission of sentence for good conduct, and if the lieutenant governor in council has made rules for keeping a correct record of such conduct, the governor general in council may, by proclamation, declare these sections in force within such province from and after the day named in such proclamation.
While the word "province" in these sections, by virtue of the Interpretation Act, includes both the Northwest Territories and the Yukon Territory, there is an absence of rules made by the lieutenant governor of the province in those two territories, because there is not any lieutenant governor. The purpose of clause 1 is to make it clear that, in those two territories where there is no lieutenant governor of a province, the necessary rules can be provided by action of the governor general in council.
[Mr. Garson.l

Then as to clause 2 of the bill, from time to time over the years various amendments and additions have been made to the act in order to provide for special types of institutions in the various provinces. For example, in the province of Ontario there is the Ontario reformatory and the Andrew Mercer reformatory for female prisoners; and as of recent date, there is a new type of prison in British Columbia known as the New Haven. The occasion of this clause 2 being before the chamber is that on November 18,	1950, the deputy attorney
general of Alberta wrote to the Department of Justice a letter from which I should like to quote. He said:
In this province-
That is, Alberta.
-we are establishing a new penal institution at Bowden and it is proposed that first offenders and persons who have committed minor offences might be screened out of our jails and sent to this institution which will be operated somewhat along the lines of the prison farms in the province of Ontario.
In order to enable the province to transfer prisoners to this new institution, I think it is necessary to make provision for the same in the Prisons and Reformatories Act and I have drafted a new part to the act to be made applicable to the province of Alberta.
It is, of course, pursuant to this request that clause 2 is introduced in the present amending bill.

subtopic: STATUTORY REMISSION OF SENTENCES, NORTHWEST AND YUKON TERRITORIES, AND CUSTODIAL CARE, ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaket, from what the minister has said, I understand that this bill, under the new section 18, gives to the governor in council discretion to declare a prison in a province to be of such a character that sections 19, 20 and 21 of the Prisons and Reformatories Act, 1927, might well be applied to it; and further, gives to the governor in council the power to declare those sections in force with regard to that particular prison.
In those provinces which qualify, there is an opportunity for a prisoner to earn certain remission of the sentence to which he has been condemned. Apparently, among the qualifications of these prisons, there must be in that prison provision, for the keeping of a correct daily record of every prisoner in such prison. The terms of the clause are as follows:
(b) rules for keeping a correct record of the daily conduct of every prisoner in such prison, noting his behaviour, industry, diligence and faithfulness and the strictness with which he observes the prison regulations . . .
I have put that on the record for the purpose of saying that, in my opinion, that is a great achievement if it will be applied in many of these institutions, because it implies a study of the individual. It is a final admission that it is only upon the basis of the study of the individual that we can put

into effect a reform rather than a punitive approach. In other words, a reform program will have to be handled on the basis of the individual, whereas a mere punitive program could be handled on the treatment of the mass.
As I sat here this evening, thinking about this subject, I sent for a copy of Hansard for November 15, 1945. My mind harks back to the very fine speech made by the late member for Kindersley. I thought it was a memorable speech. While I did not have time to read all of it this evening, I did jot down one or two of the points made by the late Mr. Jaenicke on that occasion. I have noted that he praised the Archambault report and said in connection with it:
Our penitentiary system is more a system of punishment than a system of paying attention to the reformation of the convict.
And later:
Our present system makes real habitual criminals out of those who could be reformed and made useful members of society.
He stated further that there had been no attempt at segregation. Incidentally, Mr. Jaenicke had made a practical study of the matter by visiting Kingston penitentiary, and I believe certain others. In that connection he said:
I find that no real progress has been made with respect to education since the commission made its report.
Then he followed by a criticism of the standard of education and the standard of training of teachers in that institution. At page 2169 he said:
The most important item of reform which we need in Canada is the establishment of proper institutions for the treatment of young offenders between the ages of sixteen and twenty-one years.
He went a step farther and said he would include those up to twenty-three, as is done in England. It is on that that I would base the few general observations I should like to make about our penitentiaries, their inmateS and the manner in which I believe our present system could be improved.
Before going further I would say-and I may elaborate on this later-that our prison system has been improved over the last few years. Nowhere is the old adage of prevention being better than cure more true than in the field of penology. Treatment and re-education are replacing the old and wasteful punitive approach. When I say "wasteful" I am not thinking altogether in terms of money, but wasteful also in terms of human resources. In passing however I would direct the attention of hon. members to page 26 of the estimates where they will see that our penal system is costing us, in round figures, $9,072,000.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ABOLITION OP GOVERNOR GENERAL'S FIAT
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 192, to amend the Petition of Right Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think it may be fairly claimed that this bill represents an important step in our legal history. As is well known, all legal proceedings by the subject against the -crown in the right of Canada must be taken in the exchequer court pursuant to the Exchequer Court Act and the Petition of Right Act. The latter of these two acts requires that before the petition of right filed by the subject with the Secretary of State can be proceeded with, a governor general's fiat must first be obtained. The purpose of this bill is to abolish the necessity for securing this fiat. Thus what we propose is the abrogation of an age-old precept of our constitutional and public law. In this year 1951 we are writing the final chapter in the history of an important legal doctrine which can be traced back to the time of Edward I.
The purpose of this legislation is to place the crown in right of Canada- in petition of right proceedings in the exchequer court in substantially the same position as an ordinary



Petition of Right Act
litigant. This will be accomplished by removing the necessity of obtaining a fiat before a petition of right can be proceeded with. If this bill be passed, as I am sure it will be, it will be possible for a citizen under the Petition of Right Act to institute proceedings against the crown in the exchequer court without the crown's consent given by fiat, just as individuals now conduct litigation against one another in that court.
In order to make the new right of the citizen more effective, the bill also provides in other respects for simplification of procedure in the exchequer court. The result of the bill will be to provide a citizen with a simple, direct, and as far as possible economical method of proceeding as of right against the crown. Since the bill marks a new phase in our legal and constitutional development, it seems appropriate for me to describe briefly its historical background. Its historical setting can be traced, as I have already indicated, to the time of Edward I in the thirteenth century, although its origin undoubtedly extends to even more ancient times. Both the legal theory and the rule of procedure adopted in consequence of that theory are now being discarded by this bill.
In their historical origin our courts were the king's courts. They were created by the king to hear and determine suits brought between subject and subject in accordance with rules of the common law. Since the courts had been created by the king and, in a very real sense, represented the monarchy in the exercise of its judicial function, it was not possible for a subject to sue the king in his own courts. However, even in those early medieval times subjects occasionally had legal claims against the crown and, since they could not sue the king in his own courts, subjects could only hope to get redress by petitioning the king for justice. Thus from very early times these petitions addressed to the king for the redress of wrongs committed by his officers have been known, as they are known in Canada now, as petitions of right, a petition to the king that right should be done.
When the king received these petitions of right it became his practice not to decide for himself, because he had set up courts for the purpose of considering matters of that sort, whether any such petition should be granted. But the king, in relation to these petitions of right, issued an order or fiat addressed to his own courts directing in effect: Let justice be done. In this way issues between the crown and subjects were brought before the courts and there determined in accordance with the law. That is the sole basis in 1951

on which petitions of right against His Majesty in the right of Canada are decided in this country.
It is this old doctrine of constitutional and public law which the government is now asking parliament to abrogate. From this point on, with the passage of this measure, the crown in proceedings in the exchequer court will be in substantially the same position as a subject. It will no longer be necessary for a subject with a claim against the crown to ask for a fiat from the crown before his case can be heard. While the taking of this step marks the formal end of an ancient legal rule, this legal change in a way is a recognition of what is already in substance an accomplished fact. It hardly needs to be said that the crown and the executive arm of government are today in no sense comparable to what they were in the thirteenth century under Edward I. The progress of our constitutional history from the day when the theory of the divine right of kings prevailed, as marked by the growth of parliament and the development of responsible government, brought us to the position today where power is vested in parliament and the people. This same development has made the crown and the executive truly responsible to parliament and the people. From time to time statutes were enacted in Great Britain to assimilate the procedure by petition of right to the ordinary procedure in the courts. That was a development in our courts parallel to the development which was taking place in parliament and in our constitution.
Soon after confederation this parliament enacted legislation designed to facilitate the trial of matters between the crown and the subject.
The first Petition of Right Act was enacted in 1876 and established the basic principle that the procedure in cases between the crown and the subject should be assimilated to that of ordinary litigation; that is to say that apart from this necessity of getting a fiat, once the fiat was obtained and the case before the courts, from that point on the proceedings were pretty much as in ordinary litigation.
In 1887 parliament created the exchequer court as the appropriate forum for the hearing of matters within the legislative jurisdiction of parliament including matters between His Majesty in the right of Canada on the one hand and any subject on the other. Since that time, as is well known, both these statutes have been amended from time to time, always with the purpose of enlarging the substantive right of the subject and of facilitating and simplifying the prosecution of his claims against the crown.

All through the piece, however, it has been necessary for the subject to secure his flat before commencing his action. He has never been able to commence his action as a matter of right; and he still requires the permission of the crown to institute proceedings in the exchequer court. In earlier years the dominion did occasionally refuse to grant a fiat, but in later years such instances have become increasingly rare. For many years past it has been the invariable practice to grant a fiat; hence the subject really has not been obstructed from asserting his right by any technical advantage arising out of this ancient legal precedent. Indeed, it was found that the procedure of first requiring a fiat-and I mentioned this when the same subject matter was under debate on a previous occasion-was not without its practical advantages. While the request for the fiat was being considered it was often possible for a clearer view to be taken of the respective rights of the crown and the subject. As a result settlements were made in some cases, and unsubstantial claims were often dropped, which might not have been the case if steps had been taken automatically as will be possible from this point on. While we are now abolishing the fiat, in practice, as I have contended before and still maintain, as long as these fiats were granted almost automatically the necessity of obtaining them did not appear to work a practical hardship, and the delay occasioned by the necessity of obtaining a fiat quite often served a useful purpose.
However, in recent years the expanding role of government has given more prominence to the position of the crown as a litigant in court proceedings. As the role of government has grown its activities have impinged much more frequently upon the citizens at large, and as a result there has been some increase in the volume of litigation between the crown and the subject. The government has given careful study and consideration for some considerable time to the position as it now stands. As I have indicated, there have been several changes in the Petition of Right Act and the Exchequer Court Act, each having the effect of enlarging the right of the subject and making it easier for him to pursue it. As hon. members will recall, last session parliament adopted a special measure in respect of certain operations of a business or quasi-business nature carried on by virtually all the crown corporations of this government. That was the Statute iLaw Amendment Act, 1950. This statute placed a large number of crown corporations and agencies in the position of being amenable to the jurisdiction of Canadian courts in
Petition of Right Act
much the same way as ordinary corporations. These statutory corporations, created for the exercise of limited functions, are agents of the crown, it is true; but their activities are now governed to a large extent by the rules and laws applicable to ordinary persons and companies in the country. The legislation enacted last year, one admits at once, was directed to a more specialized problem than that raised in the present bill; but it does indicate the concern this government feels for the position of the individual citizen in this modern world, when he is confronted with the operation of government agencies in many places and in connection with his own business.
In these changes I have referred to and in the one now recommended we have had to keep in mind two important balancing factors. On the one hand -there is the obvious consideration that the citizen, as a litigant, should have an economical and effective method of pursuing his claims against the crown. I suggest, however, that this must be balanced by an equally important consideration, namely that in the interests of the general body of the citizens as taxpayers this litigation against the crown should be carried on as economically and efficiently as possible. These two balancing considerations should be taken into account not only in the substantive rights of subjects in proceedings against the crown but also in respect of the procedure to be adopted in providing remedies for those substantive rights; and it is in line with this development that the government now feels it is proper to recommend to parliament that the ancient rule of requiring a fiat before the crown itself can be sued ought to be completely abolished.
The step which is being taken in this bill follows logically from the development of our whole legal history and in particular from the successive measures that have been enacted by -this parliament since confederation. For some considerable period of time our citizens have been able to proceed against the crown as a matter of course because fiats were in no case refused. The enactment of this legislation will enable them to do so as a matter of right. This bill, therefore, represents a real milestone in the development of our law and our constitution. It represents a clear recognition of the realities of our modern life; and its enactment will not only make it easier for a citizen to pursue his claim against the crown but will give all people absolute assurance that in the conduct of its operations the government is not sheltering behind a refusal to grant a necessary fiat.

Petition of Right Act Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Lake Centre): Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the minister and the government on the change of heart that has taken place with respect to the subject of this bill. It is not long ago that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) pointed out in this house that there was really no need for the removal of this bar to the right of the subject to equality in the courts. My memory recalls when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stated that as far as he was concerned he would not agree to the introduction in this house of any measure that would remove the necessity of the subject petitioning for the issue of a flat whose formula reads "let justice be done". I congratulate the government on having gone as far as it has, though my optimism does not equal that of the minister when he claims that the subject in the king's courts is now on terms of equality with the king.
Before dealing in general with this bill I would say to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that I have some doubts as to whether his manner of introducing this bill will give legality to the bill when it becomes law. As the minister has stated, since the days of Edward I the king has been in the position of superiority in so far as his relations with his subjects are concerned. One of the few prerogative rights remaining to His Majesty the King is his right not to be sued in the king's courts excepting with his leave and fiat. I feel the minister should give consideration to acquainting the house with the fact that His Excellency the Governor General has consented to this bill being introduced, for without that consent I doubt whether this bill can lawfully be passed by parliament.
Mr. Speaker, in the introduction of money resolutions there is a formula that is always used'. A member of the king's cabinet invariably announces that the governor general has been made aware of the contents of this resolution, and recommends it to the consideration of the house. In the bill providing for the removal of the need of a petition of right, unless the governor general has been apprised of this bill and has consented to it, His Majesty and his representative are without consent, being divested of a prerogative that cannot be removed without that consent. By way of illustration I should like to indicate for the information of the Minister of Justice the manner in which similar legislation was introduced in the United Kingdom. On March 4, 1947, the crown proceedings bill was introduced by Viscount Jowitt, the lord chancellor, who used these words:
In moving the second reading of the bill, I have it in command to acquaint the house that His Majesty the King, having been informed of the contents of

the Crown Proceedings bill, is prepared to place the interests of the crown at the disposal of parliament in, connection with the bill.
I waited, and I waited patiently, for the minister to make a similar statement, for I doubt whether the prerogative of His Majesty the King, of not being sued except by his consent, can be taken away by the House of Commons and the other place without the consent of the governor general as the representative of the king.
When the same bill came before the House of Commons, even though in the House of Lords the formula had been used by the lord chancellor, the attorney general, Sir Hartley Shawcross, in moving the second reading himself realized the need of the king consenting to the removal of one of his prerogatives which goes back to medieval days. He used these words:
I have it in command from the king to acquaint the house that His Majesty, having been informed of the contents of the Crown Proceedings bill, is prepared to place the interests of the crown at the disposal of parliament in connection with the bill.
In my opinion the Minister of Justice will have to give consideration to a similar formula being used in this house, and also to the need of acquainting the governor general with the fact that the House of Commons is desirous of removing one of the prerogative powers of His Majesty the King, After all, the right not to be sued is one of the great remaining prerogatives of the king, and it goes back to the days of Edward I. The king's courts were and have continued to be available to the subjects of the king in litigation as between the subjects of the king, but denied to the subjects of the king against him because "the king can do no wrong." There should be no failure to carry out every fundamental constitutional requirement, for by this legislation parliament will take from the king a power and prerogative that antedates our own constitutional development and carries us back in the British tradition to the year 1347.
I agree with the minister when he says that this is an important constitutional change but with the qualification that it does not go as far as it should. It allows the subject in Canada, without the necessity of a fiat, to take proceedings for such matters as have hitherto required a fiat. It does not extend the right of the individual to take proceedings. His rights are covered by the Exchequer Court Act, section 18, wherein the exchequer court is given exclusive original jurisdiction in the cases set forth. Under this legislation the subject will not have the same rights against the crown that he has against the subject. He will not have the right to take

actions in tort, ini other words, civil wrongs that give rise to causes of action, except as to those torts comprised within the present provisions of the Exchequer Court Act.
In the United Kingdom when they came to wipe away this archaic survival of the doctrine of the supremacy of the king and his position above the law, the legislation granted to the subject the right to take proceedings in tort, such as for slander, for libel, malicious prosecution and for actions arising out of excessive jurisdiction on the part of courts martial convened in the name of the king. The individual, under United Kingdom act of 1947, has equal rights of action against the servants of the king for all wrongs as he would have if committed by another subject.
It is interesting to read the debate in the House of Lords. Under the act passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom the right to take proceedings in. tort was granted to every subject with a few exceptions. The Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) is in his seat and will be interested to know that the post office was specifically excepted from action for any wrongdoing in the transmission of messages. It became necessary too to except the army, navy and air force from certain types of action. For instance, as stated by Lord Jowitt, an exception was incorporated in the bill, that no action could be taken for negligence by a non-commissioned officer or soldier against a superior officer; otherwise one could conceive of an action being taken against Lord Raglan by a soldier for injuries received in the Battle of Balaklava. In the course of his remarks the lord chancellor said:
To give a simple illustration, let me take the charge of the Light Brigade. Could a trooper who took part in that charge, whose leg was shattered by a cannon-ball, have brought an action against Lord Raglan (I think it was), to recover damages on the ground that Lord Raglan had blundered?
He concluded action might be taken if not specifically denied.
After he had finished his speech Lord Raglan, a descendant of the general who gave the order at Balaklava, rose and said this:
The noble and learned viscount having referred to my great-grandfather by name, I would just like to say that his responsibility for the charge of the Light Brigade is not regarded by historians as by any means so certain as the noble and learned viscount suggested.
There was living history and tradition. The right of the subject to take action against the crown will be assured without the necessity of the issue of a fiat only so far as the restricted jurisdiction of the exchequer court
Petition of Right Act
now provides when this bill is passed but his right to sue in tort will not be widened. It will still be restricted to proceedings against the crown as provided for under the Exchequer Court Act. Having regard to the extension of government into business, referred to by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), and the many ramifications that arise by reason of the variety of relationships between emanations of the crown and the individual, I suggest that the time has come to extend to the individual in this country equality in the matter of rights of action in every respect as provided for under the act in force in the United Kingdom. Otherwise all parliament will have done is to remove what the Minister of Justice states is a mere formality, claiming as he does that seldom if at all has the crown in recent years, in the right of the Attorney General of Canada, refused any subject his right to take proceedings in the courts of law. Our constitution is constantly being changed to meet changing conditions; and this bill makes for a constitutional change to meet changing conditions.
The chief justice of Canada, the distinguished father of the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret), in a case in the supreme court provided a definition of the constitution in words that I am going to use at this moment:
The constitution of Canada does not belong either to parliament, or to the legislatures; it belongs to the country and it is there that the citizens of the country will find the protection of the rights to which they are entitled.
This constitutional change will add to the rights of Canadians.
Were one on this occasion to be inclined to self-adulation, one might point out that member after member on this side of the house has been asking for several years for the removal of this clog upon the right of the individual to take proceedings. Among them were the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), the hon. member for Eglinton. (Mr. Fleming), and the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith); and personally, I raised the matter over ten years ago. It was suggested too that when legislation was introduced to remove this archaic survival of ancient days in our constitution, the rights of the individual should be extended beyond those that now exist, and that the subject should be placed in equality with regard to the king as he is in actions that can be taken against fellow citizens. In modern days the principle of requiring a fiat has become indefensible. The king was and is the fountain of justice, yet when an action is to be taken, justice could be refused fay the custodian of the king's conscience. That

Petition of Right Act requirement has now been removed and that is a step forward. For that step I congratulate the Minister of Justice. But at the same time I suggest that having gone so far along the road in extending to the subject equality with the king, one thing more remains to be done, namely to extend the rights of the individual so that there will, in fact, be in the king's court equality of the individual with the king and his representatives.
My hon. and learned friend also avers that procedure has been simplified and that one of the aims of this legislation is to assure economy to the subject seeking the king's justice and also at the same time to assure economy in so far as the taxpayer is concerned. With those two objectives I agree; but I submit that in order to secure economy and in order to extend the ambit of the field of justice to individuals in our country, wherever they may live, another step should be taken, namely to abolish the exclusive jurisdiction now possessed by the exchequer court and the giving to the subject of the alternative right to proceed against the crown in the ordinary courts of the land.
Furthermore in simplifying procedure, rules should be made-and I think they would have to be passed by parliament-to enable discovery of documents as against the crown. The individual in an action against the crown has the right to ask for the discovery of documents; but His Majesty's ministers have the right to say that it is not in the public interest to produce the documents asked for. I feel that the right of the minister to exercise that authority in the public interest should be circumscribed to a certain extent. Certainly the safety of the state and the public interest are of foremost consideration. But the minister, representing one of the crown corporations of our country, in actions against the crown corporation, should not be allowed to raise as an answer to the request for the production of documents that it is not in the public interest to produce those documents, without having those documents produced to the judge trying the case so that he himself may conclude whether there is foundation for the claim or reservation made by the minister.
I can think of two or three cases against the wheat board, and other emanations of the crown, wherein the stand has been taken that it is not in the public interest to produce documents. That excuse might be used as a means whereby documents are not to be produced, because of the fact that the interests of the government might sometimes be regarded by ministers as the interest of


the state. I feel some measure in that regard should be brought into being in order to simplify the procedure.
There have been two cases in connection with the discovery of documents as against the crown, neither of which I have looked up for the present debate, but I recollect the events and ciroumstances connected with them. In one case from Australia there was an appeal in connection with the refusal on the part of the minister to produce documents of a crown corporation, on the ground that it was not in the public interest. The privy council held that when a minister avowed it was not in the public interest, that was the end. On the other hand during the days of the war, the First Lord of the Admiralty refused to produce certain documents on the ground that it was not in the public interest to produce them. The House of Lords held that the documents had to be produced to the trial judge who, after perusal, would conclude whether or not there was a sound basis for the refusal on the part of the king's minister to produce a document.
I am not going into anything controversial on this occasion, but it is conceivable that a refusal to produce documents by a crown corporation could result in a denial of justice within the king's courts. The decision that the public interest would deny the production of a document should rest with the judiciary.
The minister very properly stated that business and government, or government in business, is expanding at a very great rate -and that is true. The rights of the subject are being diminished as the powers of the executive are being increased. We find year after year that the executive has been entrenching upon the rights of the individual and, in statutes and also by orders in council, has been denying the right of the individual to question in the courts of law any act performed by a minister of the crown under a statute or order in council, or by anyone acting through or under him.
Sir, if our democracy is to mean freedom of the individual, then no citizen should be denied the right of appeal to the courts when, in the opinion of that citizen, an injustice has been done. In introducing this measure the minister has granted a right to the individual which, as he has said, was almost ephemeral in so far as its material existence was concerned. He would perpetuate his name as a great minister of justice were he to insist that no statute or order in council, wherein the right of an individual to appeal to the courts is denied, would longer be countenanced by him or the government.

I think of several orders in council which provide that no individual citizen in this country could lodge any proceedings against the crown for wrongdoings. The opposition took a strong stand in that behalf when the Foreign Exchange Control Act came before the house and a section was inserted in the act which provided that where there was wrongdoing on the part of the officials of the crown under that act a citizen could take proceedings, but would be restricted to nominal damages, and no costs.
I suggest to the minister that, having regard to his desire as expressed tonight to assure to the individual equality before the law, he should take the bureaucrats off the pedestals they sit upon, immune from responsibility to the courts, and place them in a position where citizens whose rights have been interfered with illegally shall have recourse to the courts when injustice has been done to them. That would be a step along the road toward raising the status of the citizen. To use the minister's expression, that would, be a milestone in the achievement of the rights of the individual.
While parliament sits, orders in council are still being issued placing ministers of the crown in a position of absolute power. The king's courts are being denied to those whose rights are interfered with. I have in my hand an order in council dated May 16, 1951, dealing with priority regulations, the purpose of which is a good one. It grants to the minister the power requiring any person who produces or deals in or has in his possession any essential supplies to deal with them, as directed and to furnish information as directed.
Those powers may be necessary, although I cannot justify the right of a minister to place a minister or a bureaucrat above the law. The order in council contains the following term:
Where any person fails to fulfil any contract or obligation whether made or assumed before or after the effective date of these regulations, and such failure is due to compliance on the part of such person with any order made under the authority of these regulations after such contract or obligation was made or assumed, proof of that fact shall be a good defence to any action or proceeding against such person in respect of such failure.
While parliament is sitting a minister of the crown by order in council is granted the power to decide that where a breach of contract takes place, where the rule of law has been abrogated the fact that a breach of contract resulted from his orders shall be a defence in the courts of law. In my opinion power such as that above the courts should
Petition of Right Act
not be entrusted to a mere human being, no matter how high his position in the ministry of the country may be.
Under this bill the rights to sue the crown without leave in the courts of the land will be granted to the individual, and the fiction that the king can do no wrong, which goes back, as the minister has said, to the days when the king was absolute, when justice was an emanation of the crown, will be terminated. Parliament should go further and remove the unjustifiable abrogation of the right of the individual which places a minister of the crown or anyone acting on behalf of the minister above the king's courts.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Dion in the chair.
